title: Quantifying Student Success with Generative AI: A Monte Carlo Simulation Informed by Systematic Review
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the methodological problem of how to quantify students’ perceived success with generative AI tools in higher education when most existing studies report only survey summaries rather than raw learner-level data. The author asks how findings from a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review can be converted into a probabilistic, composite indicator of student success. The paper defines “success” operationally as students’ self-evaluated success in using generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in educational settings, rather than objective academic performance or grades.

The study uses a hybrid approach: a systematic review of Scopus-indexed empirical studies on student perceptions of generative AI in higher education (2023–2025), followed by Monte Carlo simulation based on published item-level means and standard deviations. Nineteen empirical articles met the inclusion criteria, and six provided complete item-level Likert statistics suitable for modelling. From those, one 10-item usability instrument from a prior health sciences education study was selected as a canonical dataset. Its items were reorganized into three themes—Ease of Use & Learnability, System Efficiency & Learning Burden, and Perceived Complexity & Integration—and used to simulate 10,000 synthetic learners. Inverse-variance weighting and Bessel-corrected variance estimates were used to generate a composite perception-based “Success Score.”

The population and context are higher education students, drawn indirectly through the reviewed literature rather than through a newly collected participant sample in this paper. The paper discusses university students broadly, with variation across disciplines and levels of study noted in the reviewed evidence. The implementation context is not a real-world classroom intervention but a privacy-preserving modelling exercise using published summary statistics. The selected canonical input dataset came from higher education use of ChatGPT/GenAI, but this paper itself does not report a single live deployment setting, intervention duration, or teacher-mediated implementation.

The main conclusion is that the proposed simulation framework can transparently translate survey-based perception data into a reproducible composite measure of perceived student success with generative AI. Under the baseline inverse-variance weighting scheme, System Efficiency & Learning Burden had the largest influence on the simulated Success Score, while Ease of Use & Learnability and Perceived Complexity & Integration also contributed positively but less strongly. The author emphasizes that the resulting score is a perception-based proxy, not a direct measure of academic achievement, and argues that the framework is useful for benchmarking GenAI tools in higher education when individual-level data are unavailable.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM used for conversational assistance and content generation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper does not evaluate ChatGPT outcomes directly in a new student experiment. It uses a 10-item usability instrument from Veras et al. (2024) on ChatGPT as the canonical input for a Monte Carlo simulation that models a perception-based student 'Success Score' from published summary statistics.

findings.finding_summary: Using the ChatGPT usability instrument from Veras et al. (2024) as the canonical dataset, the simulation produced a tightly concentrated perception-based Success Score distribution with mean = 4.0666, SD = 0.0956, and IQR = 4.0032–4.1308 on a 1–5 scale, interpreted as generally favourable self-evaluations of success when using GenAI tools. This is a simulation-derived perception proxy rather than a direct academic performance measure.
findings.measure: Simulated perception-based Success Score on a 1–5 Likert-derived scale

findings.finding_summary: In regression on the simulated data, System Efficiency & Learning Burden was the strongest contributor to the composite Success Score under inverse-variance weighting (beta = 0.7823, p < 0.001), compared with Ease of Use & Learnability (beta = 0.0856, p < 0.001) and Perceived Complexity & Integration (beta = 0.1381, p < 0.001). Model fit was R2 = 0.724 with F(3, 9996) = 8741, p < 0.001.
findings.measure: Regression coefficients linking usability themes to simulated Success Score

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic-review-informed simulation paper using published summary statistics rather than a direct empirical comparison of student outcomes. The reported results are model-based and perception-focused, not causal estimates of learning gains.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports favorable simulated perception scores and strong model coefficients, but these are not direct effect sizes on academic outcomes. Impact on learning is therefore suggestive but unclear.
